title: PhD Scholarship at La Trobe University: Research Opportunity on Family Violence Safety for First Nations and Culturally Diverse Families
summary: La Trobe University is offering a prestigious PhD scholarship opportunity for a doctoral researcher interested in family violence, family court systems, cultural safety, Indigenous and culturally and linguistically diverse families, child and family wellbeing, and long-term safety outcomes. The scholarship forms part of a major Australian Research Council (ARC) Discovery Project examining how safety from domestic and family violence develops and changes for parents involved in family court litigation. The successful PhD candidate will have the opportunity to contribute to an important body of research investigating what helps parents and children move from situations of high risk toward sustained safety, particularly among First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CALD) families . The PhD will be based at La Trobe University and will be supported by experienced researchers from the University s Bouverie Centre, alongside cultural consultants and collaborators connected with the Australian family court system. PhD Scholarship Overview This doctoral opportunity is particularly suited to applicants who are passionate about understanding family violence and improving outcomes for families navigating complex legal, social and service systems. The research will focus on experiences of safety among First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse parents who have been involved in family court proceedings. Rather than looking only at the presence of family violence or the level of risk experienced by families, the research seeks to understand a broader and equally important question: What helps families become safer after initially being identified as being at high risk? The successful candidate will investigate the personal, family, cultural, community, service and court-related factors that may contribute to improved and sustained safety. This is an opportunity to undertake doctoral research that combines academic research with real-world implications for family courts, family violence services, communities, parents and children. Scholarship Value The scholarship provides: $36,000 per year Funding for 3.5 years Full-time PhD study Research opportunities connected to a major ARC-funded Discovery Project Supervision from experienced researchers in family violence, family court processes and research methodology Opportunities to develop expertise in culturally appropriate research methods Access to the research environment of La Trobe University s Bouverie Centre Opportunities to contribute to research intended to improve safety outcomes for families involved in the family law system The scholarship is funded through La Trobe University s contribution to the ARC Discovery Project. About the ARC Discovery Project The PhD is connected to the Australian Research Council Discovery Project titled: “Enhancing Safety from Family Violence Through and Beyond Family Court Litigation.” The wider project will investigate experiences of safety from domestic and family violence among parents involved in Australia s family court system. The project is designed to follow families over a period of four years after entry into the family court system , allowing researchers to examine what happens not only while families are under the supervision of the court but also after the court s direct involvement decreases or ends. This longer-term approach is important because safety can change over time. A family that is considered high risk when entering court may experience different circumstances several months or years later. The research therefore seeks to understand: How safety changes over time. Which factors are associated with improved safety. Which factors are associated with continued risk. Whether court-based triage processes contribute to improved safety. How family, cultural, personal and social circumstances influence safety. How court management and family circumstances interact. What parents themselves identify as contributing to improved safety. What personal and service-related costs are associated with achieving sustained safety. Focus of the PhD Research The PhD will specifically investigate Research Question 2d of the wider ARC Discovery Project: “To what do First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse parents attribute improved safety after initial high risk?” The doctoral candidate will have an opportunity to refine the precise research questions in collaboration with the supervisory team. The research may explore several important areas. 1. Factors that support sustained safety The research will examine the factors that help families achieve and maintain safety. These factors could include: Family relationships. Community support. Cultural connections. Access to appropriate services. Personal circumstances. Social support. Interactions with government and statutory systems. Family court processes. Safety planning. Service responses to family violence. Connections to country and community. Experiences of children and parents. Access to culturally appropriate support. The study will consider whether these factors operate differently for First Nations families and culturally and linguistically diverse families. 2. Experiences of mothers following high-risk assessments Another important aspect of the research concerns how First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse mothers experience safety when they have previously been identified as being at high risk. The research will seek to understand their experiences over time rather than examining safety at only one point. This can provide a deeper understanding of how circumstances change during and after family court proceedings. 3. Parents explanations of improved safety The PhD will also explore how parents themselves explain changes in their circumstances. Instead of relying exclusively on professional assessments or administrative data, the research will provide an opportunity for parents to describe: What changed in their lives. What they believe helped them become safer. Which services were helpful. Which services were difficult or harmful. The role of family and community. The importance of culture. The role of country and connection. Their experiences with the family court. Their interactions with statutory systems. Their experiences after court involvement decreased. What helped them protect themselves and their children. This approach is intended to provide a richer understanding of family safety from the perspective of people who have experienced these circumstances themselves. Expected Research Approaches and Methods The PhD is expected to use several complementary research approaches. The successful candidate will work with the supervisory team to refine the research questions and develop culturally informed methodologies appropriate for the study population. The proposed PhD-by-publication may involve three major approaches. 1. Review of global Family Court practices The first component may involve examining family court practices internationally. The research will investigate practices involving Indigenous and culturally and linguistically diverse populations that seek to improve: Cultural safety. Physical safety. Psychological safety. Family safety. Access to justice. Appropriate engagement with court processes. Support for parents and children. Responsiveness to cultural and community contexts. This component could help identify practices that may contribute to safer experiences for families throughout family court litigation. 2. Analysis of existing research data The second component will involve analysis of data that has already been collected. The available dataset contains information on 214 First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse parents and their initial safety profiles when they entered the court system. The candidate may compare these initial safety profiles with those of non-Indigenous parents and examine patterns that could contribute to understanding differences in risk and safety. This provides an opportunity for the PhD candidate to develop advanced skills in research data analysis and interpretation. 3. Yarning and narrative approaches The third component is expected to involve a yarning approach with existing cohort participants. Yarning can provide an opportunity for participants to share their experiences through culturally appropriate forms of conversation. In this research, the approach is intended to help participants tell their unfolding stories of safety over time. The research will explore the role of: Community. Country. Family. Service systems. Government and statutory systems. Family courts. Personal experiences. Relationships. Cultural identity and connection. Experiences of risk and safety. Other narrative methods may also be considered. The project specifically notes that approaches such as drawings and artwork are encouraged where appropriate. This creates an opportunity for the research to move beyond conventional interview-based methods and explore ways of allowing participants to communicate experiences of safety in forms that are meaningful to them. Why This PhD Research Is Important Domestic and family violence can have long-lasting effects on parents and children, particularly when families are involved in complex legal proceedings. Family court litigation can itself be a challenging experience, especially for people who are already dealing with violence, trauma, separation, parenting disputes and concerns about the safety of their children. For First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse families, additional cultural, social and systemic considerations may influence how they experience the court system and services around it. Understanding these experiences is therefore essential for developing approaches that are not only legally appropriate but also culturally responsive and genuinely focused on safety. The research could contribute to improved understanding of: How families move from high-risk circumstances toward greater safety. Why some families experience improved outcomes while others continue to experience risk. How culture influences experiences of safety. How community and family relationships contribute to wellbeing. How service systems can better support families. How family courts can respond more effectively to diverse communities. How culturally appropriate research methods can improve understanding of family violence. How parents and children can be better supported during and after court proceedings. Research Supervisors The PhD candidate will be supervised by a multidisciplinary research team with expertise in family violence, family relationships, research methodology and family court-related research. Primary Supervisor: Dr Anna Booth Dr Anna Booth will serve as the Primary Supervisor for the PhD project. Co-Supervisors The candidate will also be supported by: Dr Felicity Painter Professor Jennifer McIntosh Together, the supervisors will provide expertise in research methodology, analysis and the broader field of family violence and family court research. They will also assist the candidate in developing research outputs and publishing findings from the project. Cultural Support and Research Mentoring An important feature of this PhD opportunity is the emphasis on culturally appropriate research. The candidate will receive cultural support and consultation from Alison Elliott , Bouverie s First Nations team leader. The research team will also encourage links with the Family Courts Indigenous Advisor at the Melbourne Registry . This support is particularly relevant because the project involves research with First Nations families and requires approaches that are respectful, culturally informed and appropriate for the communities involved. The candidate will also be mentored in early-career research through the Bouverie Centre at La Trobe University. They will receive support in developing knowledge of: Domestic and family violence theory. Family court research. Research methodology. Culturally appropriate research. Qualitative research approaches. Quantitative data analysis. Narrative research. Academic writing. Research publication. Working collaboratively with community and professional stakeholders. Who Can Apply? This scholarship is available to domestic applicants only . The opportunity is particularly encouraging applications from: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students who meet the University s PhD candidature requirements. Applicants whose proposed research aligns closely with the project s focus on Indigenous and culturally and linguistically diverse Australian families. The project states that if a suitable First Nations or Culturally and Linguistically Diverse candidate is not available, applications from other students whose research interests align with the project s goals may also be considered. Academic and Research Fit This opportunity may be particularly suitable for applicants with academic or professional interests in areas such as: Nursing and health sciences. Public health. Social work. Psychology. Sociology. Indigenous studies. Family studies. Social policy. Criminology. Law and family law. Child and family wellbeing. Domestic and family violence. Community development. Human services. Gender studies. Mental health and wellbeing. Research methodology. Indigenous health and wellbeing. Culturally responsive practice. Applicants should, however, assess their eligibility against La Trobe University s formal PhD admission requirements rather than relying solely on their disciplinary background. What the Successful PhD Candidate Will Do The successful candidate will become part of a broader research program examining family safety through and beyond family court litigation. Their responsibilities are expected to include: Refining the PhD research questions in collaboration with the supervisors. Developing culturally appropriate research methods. Reviewing relevant international and Australian literature. Examining global family court practices. Analysing existing research data. Investigating safety profiles of First Nations and culturally and linguistically diverse parents. Engaging with existing research participants using appropriate approaches. Conducting qualitative and/or quantitative analyses. Exploring parents experiences and explanations of improved safety. Examining the influence of family, community, culture, country and service systems. Developing research publications. Presenting research findings through appropriate academic and professional channels. Contributing to the wider ARC Discovery Project. Completing a PhD by publication. Skills Applicants Can Develop This PhD can provide valuable research and professional development opportunities. Depending on the final research design, the candidate may develop skills in: Research design. Qualitative research. Quantitative research. Data analysis. Narrative research. Yarning methodologies. Culturally responsive research. Indigenous research approaches. Family violence research. Family court research. Academic writing. Research publication. Critical analysis. Interdisciplinary collaboration. Community-engaged research. Research ethics. Working with sensitive research topics. These skills can be valuable for future careers in academia, research institutions, government, social policy, health, family services, community organisations and other areas concerned with family wellbeing and safety. The Wider Stories of Family Safety Study The PhD is connected to the Stories of Family Safety Study , which forms part of the broader research program. The wider work is interested in understanding safety as something that can change over time. Rather than treating safety as a single outcome measured at one point, researchers seek to understand the journey families experience and the factors that contribute to changes in safety. The research therefore places considerable importance on people s lived experiences and their explanations of what helped them become safer. Background to the Research The project builds on previous research conducted by the team. This includes the ARC Linkage Project: “Family Violence Triage in Family Courts: Safety, Efficacy and Benefit.” That earlier project examined domestic and family violence screening and triage processes within Lighthouse , an innovative approach implemented by the courts to identify family violence risks among litigants. The earlier work focused on improving safety outcomes for families involved in the family law system. The new Discovery Project builds on this foundation by examining safety over a substantially longer period. This creates an opportunity to investigate what happens to families not only during their involvement with the court but also during the period after court oversight and involvement decreases. Application Process Applicants interested in the scholarship should review La Trobe University s formal requirements for applying for a research degree. The application process should be approached carefully because this is a research-based doctoral opportunity rather than a standard taught postgraduate program. Applicants should ensure that they: Meet the University s PhD candidature requirements. Confirm their domestic applicant status. Review the scholarship conditions. Consider how their academic and research background aligns with the project. Prepare the required application materials. Clearly demonstrate their interest in family violence, family safety, culturally responsive research or a closely related area. Explain how their experience and research interests align with the proposed PhD. Review the formal application instructions provided by La Trobe University. Read How to APPLY HERE Scholarship Deadline Deadline: Not specified in the information provided. Prospective applicants should not assume that the absence of a deadline means applications remain open indefinitely. It is advisable to confirm the current closing date directly with La Trobe University or the project supervisor before preparing or submitting an application. How to Get Further Information Applicants who require additional information about the scholarship or research project can contact the primary supervisor: Dr Anna Booth Email: a.booth@latrobe.edu.au Applicants can also visit the official website HERE Key Takeaways This PhD scholarship offers an opportunity to undertake doctoral research within a major ARC-funded research project focused on family violence and safety. The key features include: Degree: PhD University: La Trobe University Research centre: Bouverie Centre Scholarship: $36,000 per year Duration: 3.5 years Study mode: Full time Research focus: Safety from family violence Primary populations: First Nations and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse families Research setting: Family court and post-court contexts Methods: Potentially literature/documentary research, quantitative analysis, yarning and narrative approaches Publication: Expected PhD by publication Supervisors: Dr Anna Booth, Dr Felicity Painter and Professor Jennifer McIntosh Cultural support: Alison Elliott and connections with the Family Courts Indigenous Advisor Eligibility: Domestic applicants only First Nations applicants: Particularly encouraged to apply International applicants: Not eligible based on the information provided Deadline: Not stated; applicants should confirm directly Conclusion The La Trobe University PhD Scholarship attached to the ARC Discovery Project represents a significant opportunity for a researcher interested in family violence, family court systems, Indigenous and culturally diverse families, cultural safety and long-term family wellbeing . What makes the project particularly valuable is its focus on understanding not only why families experience risk, but also how and why safety can improve over time . By combining existing cohort data with culturally informed research approaches, including yarning and other narrative methods, the PhD candidate will have the opportunity to capture perspectives that may not be visible through conventional court or administrative data. The research could make an important contribution to family violence prevention, family court practice, culturally responsive services and policies designed to improve the safety and wellbeing of parents and children. For eligible domestic applicants with a strong interest in this area, particularly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander researchers and candidates whose work aligns with the project s focus, this is an opportunity to contribute to research with significant academic, social and practical relevance. title: IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme 2026/2027: Fully Funded Master’s Scholarship for Women in Nuclear-Related Fields
summary: The IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme (MSCFP) is an international scholarship initiative designed to encourage and support young women who want to build careers in nuclear science, nuclear technology, nuclear safety, nuclear security, nuclear medicine, nuclear law and other nuclear-related disciplines. Established by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) , the programme provides financial support to selected female students pursuing master s degrees in nuclear-related fields at accredited universities. In addition to financial assistance for master s studies, selected students may also have access to limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA. The programme is particularly valuable for women who want to develop specialist expertise in a field where women remain underrepresented and subsequently contribute to the peaceful, safe and secure applications of nuclear science and technology. The IAEA MSCFP is therefore more than a conventional university scholarship. It is an opportunity to obtain advanced academic training while positioning yourself for a future career in the international nuclear sector. About the IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme The IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme was created to inspire more young women to pursue educational and professional opportunities in nuclear-related fields. The programme recognizes the importance of developing a highly skilled workforce capable of contributing to the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology. Through the MSCFP, selected students receive financial assistance toward their master s studies in approved nuclear-related disciplines. The programme may also provide limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA, allowing eligible students to gain exposure to professional environments connected to their academic specialization. The initiative is named after Marie Skłodowska-Curie , one of history s most influential scientists and a pioneer in the study of radioactivity. The programme s broader objective is to encourage the next generation of women scientists, engineers, researchers, legal experts and professionals to enter and contribute to the nuclear field. The IAEA has reported substantial participation in the programme since its launch. Its 2025 reporting stated that 760 students from 129 Member States had been selected since the programme began in 2020, with recipients studying in 76 countries. What Does the IAEA MSCFP Scholarship Cover? One of the major attractions of the IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme is the level of financial support available to successful applicants. Selected students may receive: Up to €20,000 for tuition costs Up to €20,000 for living costs Potential internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA Exposure to an international professional and academic network in nuclear-related fields This means that the maximum support described under the programme can reach up to €40,000 , consisting of up to €20,000 toward tuition and up to €20,000 toward living expenses. The actual amount awarded can depend on the applicant s circumstances and the programme s assessment of the financial support required. Applicants who already have another scholarship for their master s programme must declare it to the IAEA. Where additional scholarship funding exists, the IAEA s financial support may be adjusted accordingly. The programme s financial arrangements are therefore designed to prevent undisclosed duplication of scholarship support. Who Can Apply for the IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship? The MSCFP has specific eligibility requirements, and applicants should carefully review them before beginning an application. 1. Applicants must be female The programme is specifically designed to encourage more women to pursue careers in nuclear-related disciplines. Therefore, the programme is open to female candidates who meet the academic and programme requirements. 2. Applicants must be from an IAEA Member State The programme is open to students from IAEA Member States . This means that eligibility is determined by the applicant s country being a Member State of the International Atomic Energy Agency rather than by a particular continent or region. Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Middle East, the Pacific and other regions may therefore be eligible if their country is an IAEA Member State. 3. Applicants must be accepted into or enrolled in a master s programme Applicants must either: Have been accepted into an accredited university master s programme; or Already be enrolled in an accredited university master s programme. The master s programme must be related to an eligible nuclear-related field. An applicant who has not yet secured admission to an eligible master s programme should therefore pay particular attention to the admission requirement before applying. Academic Requirements Academic performance is an important component of the MSCFP selection process. The programme indicates that preference is given to candidates with above-average academic credentials , specifically: 75% or above , or A GPA greater than 3.0 out of 4.0 . Meeting the academic benchmark does not necessarily mean an applicant will automatically receive the fellowship. Selection also considers other factors, including educational background, previous achievements, motivation, career objectives and commitment to public service. Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that academic grades alone determine the outcome. Eligible Fields of Study The IAEA MSCFP supports master s programmes in fields connected to nuclear science, nuclear technology and the wider peaceful applications of nuclear energy. Eligible or relevant fields include areas such as: Nuclear Engineering Nuclear engineering focuses on the design, operation, safety and technological development of nuclear systems and facilities. Students interested in reactor technology, nuclear energy systems and related engineering applications may find this field particularly relevant. Nuclear Physics Nuclear physics examines the properties, structure and interactions of atomic nuclei. It is an important foundation for many applications of nuclear science and technology. Nuclear Chemistry Nuclear chemistry involves the study of radioactive materials, nuclear reactions, radioisotopes and chemical processes associated with nuclear science. Nuclear Medicine Nuclear medicine uses radioactive materials for diagnosis, imaging and treatment of disease. This area is particularly relevant to students interested in the intersection between healthcare and nuclear technology. Isotopic Techniques Isotopic techniques have applications across areas such as medicine, agriculture, environmental science, hydrology, food safety and scientific research. Radiation Biology Radiation biology examines the effects of ionizing radiation on living organisms and biological systems. This field is important in areas including radiation protection, medicine and nuclear research. Nuclear Safety Nuclear safety focuses on preventing accidents and minimizing risks associated with nuclear facilities, materials and technologies. Nuclear Security Nuclear security concerns measures designed to prevent, detect and respond to unauthorized access, theft, misuse or other malicious activities involving nuclear and radioactive materials. Nuclear Non-Proliferation Nuclear non-proliferation deals with efforts to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons while supporting peaceful applications of nuclear technology. Nuclear Law Nuclear law combines legal principles with the regulatory requirements surrounding nuclear activities. It can involve areas such as nuclear safety, nuclear security, liability, safeguards, regulation and international nuclear cooperation. The IAEA provides a broader list of eligible and related fields, meaning applicants should not automatically assume that their programme is ineligible simply because its title does not exactly match one of the examples above. Why the Field of Study Matters Applicants should understand that the MSCFP is not a general master s scholarship. The programme is specifically connected to the IAEA s mandate and therefore focuses on disciplines that can contribute to the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology. For example, a general master s programme that has no meaningful connection to nuclear science, technology, safety, security, medicine, law or another relevant area may not qualify. Applicants should therefore carefully compare their intended programme with the IAEA s list of supported fields before applying. Required Application Documents Applicants are required to submit supporting documents in addition to completing the online MSCFP application form. The required documents include the following: 1. Passport or National ID Applicants must provide a copy of an accepted identification document, such as: Passport; or National identification document. Applicants should ensure that the document submitted is clear and readable. 2. University Admission or Acceptance Letter Applicants must provide an official acceptance or admission letter from the university where they will undertake their master s programme. The document should indicate: The university; The master s programme; The nuclear-related field of study; and The duration of the programme. This is an important document because the IAEA needs to establish that the applicant has been accepted into an appropriate programme. 3. Tuition Fee Statement Applicants must submit documentation showing the tuition costs associated with the master s programme. This may include an official statement or confirmation from the university detailing the applicable tuition fees. 4. Information About Other Scholarships If the applicant has received or is receiving another scholarship for the master s programme, documentation relating to that scholarship must also be submitted. Applicants are required to disclose other scholarship funding because the IAEA may adjust its financial support when another scholarship is available. 5. Reference Form Applicants must arrange for referees to complete the required IAEA reference template. At least one reference is mandatory , while a second reference is preferred . An important point is that the references must be sent directly by the referees to the MSCFP email address by the application deadline. Applicants should therefore contact their potential referees early rather than waiting until the final day of the application period. All Application Documents Must Be in English The IAEA requires application documents to be submitted in English . If an applicant s original documents are written in another language, the applicant must also provide an official English translation. This requirement is particularly important for international applicants because incomplete documentation or missing translations can affect the assessment of the application. The IAEA explicitly states that incomplete applications will not be considered . Applicants should therefore review their application carefully before submission and ensure that every required document has been provided. See Application Form HERE How the IAEA MSCFP Selection Process Works The selection process is competitive. Applications are reviewed by the IAEA MSCFP Technical Selection Committee . The committee assesses applications against several selection criteria rather than considering academic performance alone. The assessment includes: Meeting the programme s entry requirements; Educational background; Previous academic and professional achievements; Motivation for pursuing the programme; The potential impact of the fellowship on the applicant s career goals; Commitment to public service. The IAEA may also consider factors such as: Geographic diversity; Field-of-study diversity; Linguistic diversity; and Other programme-related considerations. This means applicants should prepare an application that tells a clear story about their academic background, professional ambitions and intended contribution to the nuclear field. What Should Applicants Emphasize in Their Applications? Because the selection process goes beyond grades, applicants should make sure their application clearly explains why they want to pursue a nuclear-related career . A strong application should demonstrate a logical connection between: Previous education → chosen master s programme → nuclear-related career goals → potential impact on society → commitment to public service. Applicants should also explain how receiving the fellowship could help them contribute to their country, region or the wider international community. For example, an applicant interested in nuclear medicine could explain how advanced training could contribute to improved access to nuclear diagnostic or therapeutic technologies. Similarly, someone interested in nuclear safety could explain how specialist training could contribute to stronger safety systems, regulation or technical capacity. Internship Opportunities The MSCFP also provides limited internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA. These opportunities can provide students with exposure to professional environments connected to nuclear science and technology. The IAEA has reported that MSCFP graduates have subsequently been confirmed for internships within IAEA departments and laboratories as well as external organizations, including IAEA Collaborating Centres and other public and private sector partners. Internship opportunities can be particularly valuable because they may allow students to complement academic study with practical professional exposure. However, applicants should understand that the fellowship s primary purpose is master s-level study and that internship opportunities are described as limited . Commitment to Public Service Commitment to public service is one of the factors considered during the selection process. This is significant because the programme is intended not simply to finance individual education but to contribute to the development of a skilled workforce capable of supporting the safe, secure and peaceful use of nuclear science and technology. Applicants should therefore consider how their education and future career can contribute to areas such as: Public health; Nuclear safety; Radiation protection; Energy security; Scientific research; Environmental protection; Nuclear security; Nuclear regulation; Nuclear medicine; Food and agriculture; Water resources; International cooperation; or Other peaceful applications of nuclear technology. Financial Support and Other Scholarships Applicants who already have financial support from another scholarship must disclose that funding to the IAEA. The IAEA explains that its financial support may be reduced where another scholarship exists. In particular, the IAEA may provide only tuition support rather than both tuition and living-cost support for the relevant period. Transparency is therefore essential. Applicants should not omit information about other scholarships in an attempt to receive additional funding. Failure to provide relevant information in a timely and transparent manner may lead to suspension of the IAEA s financial support. Fellowship Acceptance Successful applicants will receive an offer from the IAEA. Selected candidates are required to confirm acceptance of the fellowship within one week . The fellowship offer will contain important information concerning: The value of the award; Payment arrangements; Expected commitments; Administrative requirements; and Other arrangements relating to the fellowship. Successful applicants should therefore carefully read the fellowship offer before accepting it. Obligation to Complete the Master s Programme The MSCFP is intended to support students through their master s education. Selected students are therefore expected to successfully complete the master s programme. Failure to graduate or failure to meet the requirements associated with the scholarship can have serious financial consequences. According to the programme information, failure to meet the scholarship requirements may result in termination of the award and an obligation to repay tuition and living-cost support received from the IAEA upon request. Applicants should therefore apply only when they are prepared to commit themselves fully to completing the master s programme. Who Should Consider Applying? The IAEA MSCFP may be particularly suitable for women who want to pursue advanced education and careers in areas such as: Nuclear engineering; Nuclear physics; Nuclear chemistry; Nuclear medicine; Radiation biology; Nuclear safety; Nuclear security; Nuclear non-proliferation; Nuclear law; Isotopic techniques; and Other fields connected to the peaceful applications of nuclear science and technology. Professional development Eligible recipients may have access to internship opportunities facilitated by the IAEA, providing potential practical exposure alongside academic study. Career development Specialized master s-level training can help prepare graduates for careers in scientific research, healthcare, engineering, regulation, nuclear safety, nuclear security, international organizations and other related sectors. Conclusion The IAEA Marie Skłodowska-Curie Fellowship Programme represents a significant opportunity for women who want to pursue advanced education and build careers in nuclear science, nuclear technology and related disciplines. With financial support of up to €20,000 for tuition and €20,000 for living costs , the programme can substantially reduce the financial burden associated with master s-level study. Beyond financial assistance, the programme can provide a pathway toward professional development and potential internship exposure within the wider international nuclear community. However, this is a specialized fellowship rather than a general master s scholarship. Applicants must be female, come from an IAEA Member State, and be accepted into or enrolled in an accredited master s programme in a nuclear-related field. Strong academic performance is preferred, with the programme indicating 75% or above or a GPA greater than 3.0/4.0 as the preferred academic benchmark. Applicants should also pay close attention to the supporting-document requirements, English-language requirements, reference process, disclosure of other scholarships and the obligation to complete the master s programme.
